schools.summary: Gill: the rulers dwelt at Jerusalem as the metropolis, for their offices, its defence, and as an example to draw the people.
Clarke: lots were cast to keep a tenth in the city, too few to man the new wall; Wesley: that the buildings be completed and the safety provided for.

Henry: the holy city was declined for three causes (stricter conversation, the post of danger, worldly advantage in the country), and replenished by rulers, volunteers, and the lot of one in ten, the tenth reckoned to God.

themes: the lot to bring one in ten

schools.summary: Gill: the willing settlers, distinguished from those taken by lot, were praised and blessed for denying themselves ease and profit.
Keil and Delitzsch: the heading names the heads of the province and its five classes (Israel, priests, Levites, Nethinim, Solomon's servants); 'province' is the land of Judah under Persia.
Clarke: volunteering was a sacrifice to patriotism in a place of danger; Wesley: they were blessed for giving up their safety and profit for a city that was the butt of its enemies' plots.

Clarke: the roll differs from 1 Chronicles 9 because it adds the companies of Ezra and Nehemiah to Zerubbabel's; Wesley: 'Israel' is a generic name, the other tribes now incorporated with Judah and Benjamin.
Ellicott: 'of the province' betrays Nehemiah the Persian official and governor; a general heading for city and country; 'Israel' generic.
Gill: the chief of the province, that is, of Judea, reduced by Babylon and now a Persian province.
Gill: the city was shared by both tribes from the first, part in Judah's lot and part in Benjamin's.

Keil and Delitzsch: two heads of Judah, Athaiah of Perez and Maaseiah of Shelah, 468 men, and the 'Shelanite' reading corrected; Ellicott: Perez given here but Zerah (present in 1 Chronicles 9) absent, perhaps a question of the text.

themes: Judah and Benjamin in one city

schools.summary: Gill: Maaseiah, perhaps the Asaiah named elsewhere, traced to Shiloni, whom he takes for Shelah.
Ellicott: 'son of Shiloni' is better 'the Shilonite,' of Shelah, youngest son of Judah; Keil and Delitzsch set the two tribes on one plan, Benjamin's heads and officers following.
Gill: the 468 were valiant men, fit to defend the city.
Henry: Judah fewer than Benjamin yet valiant, a lion's whelp; the small count a token of small beginnings.
Keil and Delitzsch: the 468 the able men of the houses of Perez and Shelah together.
Gill: the men of Benjamin who inhabited Jerusalem, the house of Sallu at their head.
Ellicott: Benjamin's two families gave the city two prefects, matching Judah; Keil and Delitzsch: two heads and 928 fathers, with chief Joel and second Judah.

themes: the tribe of Saul in the city

schools.summary: Gill: 928, more of Benjamin than Judah, from a greater share of the city or a readier will.
Henry: the greater part of Jerusalem lay in Benjamin's lot, hence the larger number.
Keil and Delitzsch: 928 the fathers of both Benjamite houses, with the tribe's officers.

debates.question: Why were there more Benjamites than men of Judah in the city?

sides.position: a greater share of the city in Benjamin's ancient lot, or a readier will to dwell there
the greater part of Jerusalem lay within Benjamin's lot by the tribal boundary

themes: the tribal boundary in the city

schools.summary: Gill: Joel the chief governor of the city.
Clarke: Joel chief magistrate, Judah his deputy; Wesley: the overseer was the captain of their thousand.
Henry: good magistrates as needful as good soldiers; a first and a second argue settled order.

debates.question: What office did Joel the overseer hold?

sides.position: chief governor or magistrate of the city
a military captain, the captain of their thousand

schools.summary: Gill: Seraiah here is called Azariah in 1 Chronicles 9:11, a variant of the same man.
Ellicott: read Jedaiah, Joiarib, Jachin as three priestly courses (1 Chronicles 9:10); Keil and Delitzsch: the 'son' before Joiarib a clerical slip.
Ellicott: Seraiah the high-priestly family name, though Eliashib was the living high priest; Keil and Delitzsch set Seraiah at the head of the ministering priests, 822.
Clarke: the ruler of the house of God had command of all secular matters, as the high priest of the spiritual.
Gill: the 822 who offered the sacrifices, burnt incense, set on the shewbread, and lighted the lamps.

themes: Seraiah ruler of the house of God

schools.summary: Gill: the 822 and their daily service of the house.
Keil and Delitzsch: Adaiah of the order of Malchiah, the courses set out one by one under one overseer.
Gill: the 242 brethren, the kinsmen of Adaiah.
Keil and Delitzsch: 'chief of the fathers' is striking, since the 242 were fathers of families, not all heads of houses.
Gill: the 128 able as priests and courageous to defend the city.
Clarke: noted for strength of body and military courage.

Ellicott: 'of valour' means able for the service of God's house, and 'son of one of the great men' is rather 'son of Haggedolim,' a proper name; Keil and Delitzsch read Zabdiel ben Haggedolim over the priests.

debates.question: What is meant by the priests being 'mighty men of valour'?

sides.position: military courage, men able to fight and defend the city
ability for the strenuous service of God's house

schools.summary: Gill: the Levites who dwelt in Jerusalem.
Keil and Delitzsch: Shemaiah of Bunni at the head, and the three divisions of Levites, over the work of the house, the outward business, and the song.
Henry: the Levites few in the city because their work was to teach through the country.

themes: few in the city, scattered to teach

schools.summary: Gill: Shabbethai and Jozabad among the chief Levites.
Ellicott: a remarkable specification of the Levites' functions, explained by the previous chapter; Keil and Delitzsch: the two set over the labour of the house of God.

Clarke (from Calmet): the outward business the victuals, victims, vestments, and vessels of the temple, the verse wanting in the Septuagint; Wesley: the gathering of contributions abroad in the country.
Henry: those over the outward concerns as needful as those given to the word and prayer.

debates.question: What was the 'outward business' of the house of God?

sides.position: the material provision within, victuals, victims, vestments, and the vessels of the temple
the gathering of the voluntary contributions and provision abroad in the country

themes: the outward business of the house

schools.summary: Clarke: Mattaniah the precentor and master-singer; Wesley: leader of the praises joined to the morning and evening sacrifice.
Gill: the Zabdi of the pedigree is the Zichri named elsewhere.
Keil and Delitzsch: Mattaniah head of the singers, Bakbukiah second, Abda of the line of Jeduthun.
Henry: thanksgiving is necessary in prayer, one to begin and the rest to follow, all done decently and in order.

themes: the singers of Asaph and Jeduthun

schools.summary: Gill: the 284 Levites resident in the city.
Keil and Delitzsch: 284 the whole body of Levites, in three divisions, far fewer than the priests' near twelve hundred.
Henry: few, because much of their work was to teach the knowledge of God through the country.

themes: the ministering tribe come home thin

schools.summary: Gill: the 172 porters, under Akkub and Talmon, who kept the gates of the temple.
Ellicott: 172 here against 212 in 1 Chronicles 9, the difference the porters of the later companies of Ezra.

Henry: the residue dwelt in the country, that the capital be filled without draining the fields; and the settlement is shadowed by the lukewarmness Malachi charged in God's name, foreshadowing the Nethinim, Levite overseer, singers, and king's commissioner of the following verses (cf. 1 Chronicles 9:6).
Gill: all the priests and Levites besides those at Jerusalem, dispersed through the towns, each in his inheritance.

themes: the residue of Israel in the cities

schools.summary: Gill: Ophel a high place or tower upon the wall.
Wesley: the Nethinim posted near the temple, because they did its servile work.
Keil and Delitzsch: Ophel the southern slope of Moriah (Neh. 3:26), the chiefs Ziha and Gispa, Bertheau's identification rejected; Ellicott: here the Nethinim are reckoned outside the wall.

themes: the given ones near the temple

schools.summary: Gill: Uzzi the supervisor of the Levites, of the line of Micha son of Asaph.
Clarke: the overseer is the visitant or inspector, rendered 'bishop' by the Septuagint and Vulgate.
Ellicott: a visitor, Uzzi a singer of Asaph, a parallel to the leader of thanksgiving in v.17; Keil and Delitzsch: the verse a supplement naming the head over Shemaiah's division of v.15.
Gill: the king either David, who ordered the singers, or the king of Persia.
Clarke: most probably Artaxerxes, a daily provision for singers who prayed as well as praised, as Darius provided for the priests (Ezra 6:10).
Ellicott: Artaxerxes gave a daily allowance beyond the exemption of Ezra 7:24, which Uzzi saw paid; Keil and Delitzsch: a royal ordinance settling a fixed daily portion.

debates.question: Whose commandment settled a daily portion on the singers?

sides.position: possibly King David, who first ordered the courses of the singers
the Persian king Artaxerxes, giving a daily maintenance out of the province

themes: a daily portion for the singers
the empire's care for the temple

schools.summary: Gill: Pethahiah of Zerah, the twin brother of Pharez.

Ellicott: his descent from Zerah makes the omission of Zerah at the chapter's head remarkable, perhaps accidental; the king's agent in the province's affairs; Keil and Delitzsch: at the king's hand, transacting business at the court.
Clarke: the governor over Jewish civil matters, who levied the tribute; Wesley: on the king's part, to judge causes and matters of tribute and grievance.

themes: the missing Zerah at the chapter's head
a Jew as the crown's officer

schools.summary: Gill: the account now passes to the country towns and their people.

Keil and Delitzsch: the 'enclosures' and 'daughters' of the towns, Kirjath-arba being Hebron (Gen. 23:2) and Jekabzeel the old Kabzeel (Josh. 15:21); Ellicott: Hebron's ancient name recovered, 'daughters' a different word from 'villages.'
Keil and Delitzsch: the southern towns from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom, named without their numbers.
Clarke: Jeshua a city nowhere else mentioned in Scripture.
Ellicott: Judah spread the length of the tribe, some fifty miles, from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom; Keil and Delitzsch: the two boundary-marks that set the compass of the resettlement.

themes: from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom
the inheritance filled corner to corner

schools.summary: Gill: Geba the southern and Michmash the northern bound, the towns named down to the valley of craftsmen, Anathoth the town of Jeremiah and Nob the city of the priests.
Ellicott: read 'from Geba to Michmash'; Keil and Delitzsch fix the sites, Geba the old boundary (2 Kings 23:8) and Aija the Aiath of Isaiah 10:28.
Clarke: Geba probably the same as Gibeah of Saul.
Keil and Delitzsch: the roll of Benjamite villages through Anathoth, Nob, and Ananiah.
Gill: Anathoth the birthplace of Jeremiah, Nob the city of the priests, and Ananiah nowhere else named.

themes: the prophet's town and the priests' city

schools.summary: Clarke: Hadid and Neballat are places unknown.
Gill: Hadid the same as Adida in the plain, Zeboim a valley of the old history, Neballat read of nowhere else.
Keil and Delitzsch: the names set in their place in the list without forcing an identification.

themes: obscure places kept in the record

schools.summary: Clarke: Lod and Ono built by the sons of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:12), the valley of craftsmen tied to 1 Chronicles 4:14.
Gill: the valley of craftsmen, the Ge-harashim of the older record, the place of the workers in wood and metal.
Keil and Delitzsch: Lod, Ono, and the valley of craftsmen close the list on the western edge, toward the plain.
Gill: the Levites scattered in both tribes for the better instruction of the people.
Clarke: the Levites' maintenance small, the service not yet fully established, and they few; the Syriac rendering rejected.
Keil and Delitzsch: divisions of Levites once of Judah now came among Benjamin; Ellicott: their fewness warranted the summary notice.

themes: the Levites in Judah and Benjamin
